content.title: About
content.content: Chia are the edible seeds of Salvia hispanica, a plant native to Mexico and Guatemala. The tiny oval seeds are light brown and have a mild nutty flavor. Chia is usually eaten dry, added to porridge, yogurt, baked goods, or beverages.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chia was a staple food for the ancient Aztec and Maya civilizations, valued for its energy‑boosting properties.
The seeds can absorb up to 12 times their weight in water, forming a gel‑like coating.
Chia is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, especially alpha‑linolenic acid (ALA).
The plant is drought‑tolerant and can grow on poor soils, making it easy to cultivate.
Since the 2010s, chia has become a popular “superfood” in Western markets.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Chia provides ALA, which supports heart health and reduces inflammation.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps stabilize blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: About 20 % of chia’s weight is protein, containing all essential amino acids.

items.title: Abundant minerals
items.content: Chia supplies calcium, magnesium, phosphorus and iron, important for bones and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolic compounds in chia help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chia seeds.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Dry seeds can become lodged in a young child’s airway; it is safer to serve them soaked or as a gel.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: High fiber intake may affect absorption of certain drugs, such as anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sprinkle chia on yogurt, smoothies, oatmeal, or incorporate into baked goods. For a classic chia pudding, soak the seeds in milk or a plant‑based drink for 10‑15 minutes until they swell into a gel.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chia seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life store them in the refrigerator. They remain good for 2‑3 years; discard if they develop a rancid or moldy odor.
